134.title: Purim: gifts and noise
134.hook: food for friends, gifts for the poor, and noise to drown out Haman's name
134.tomorrow: Passover: a seat at the seder
134.howItsDone: On Purim, Jews hear the megillah read twice, making noise at Haman's name, send mishloach manot of at least two foods to a friend, give gifts to at least two poor people, and share a festive meal.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the megillah, the scroll of Esther, where God's name never appears. Your line was hidden, not absent.

In a synagogue, someone reads a long story aloud from a scroll, and every time one particular name comes up, the whole room explodes. Kids spin wooden rattlers that sound like a flock of angry ducks. Adults stamp their feet. Someone bangs two pot lids together. The reader waits for the noise to die down, and carries on, until the name comes up again. The name is Haman. And the next morning, doorbells ring all over the neighborhood: kids in costumes, holding little baskets of cookies and candy, delivering them door to door.
screen: `A NAME, AND THE ROOM EXPLODES.` → `RATTLERS AND POT LIDS.` → `BASKETS AT THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: At the end of the book of Esther, Mordecai writes to the Jews and tells them how to keep these days forever: as "days of feasting and gladness, and of sending portions one to another, and gifts to the poor." Purim's practices come from that one verse. Sending portions, in Hebrew mishloach manot: Jewish law says at least two kinds of ready-to-eat food to at least one friend. People make whole projects of it: baskets, themes, the triangle-shaped cookies called hamantaschen. Gifts to the poor, matanot la-evyonim: money or food for at least two people in need, given on the day itself, so they can celebrate too. A festive meal in the afternoon. And hearing the megillah, evening and morning. The noise comes from an old custom of blotting out the name of Amalek, the ancient enemy the rabbis linked to Haman. The rattle is a grogger, from Yiddish. Now the teaching that changes how the whole day feels. The great twelfth-century teacher Maimonides wrote that it's better to spend more on gifts to the poor than on your own feast or on gifts to friends. Why? Because, he says, there's no greater joy than gladdening the hearts of the poor, the orphans, the widows and the strangers. The one who does that is like the Divine Presence. So Purim's joy is built in two directions at once: toward your friends, and toward people who might have nothing to celebrate with. Happiness on this day isn't complete until it's shared.

segments.voice: Think of a friend who'd be surprised by a small food gift, two simple things like a piece of fruit and a cookie, left at a door or handed over at work. Then think of someone who has less than you, and see both of them in your mind. Decide on one small thing for each.
Mishloach manot. Sending portions: gifts of food to friends on Purim, alongside gifts to the poor.
Your line: give on the happy day. The feast is for friends; the biggest share is for the poor. Day one hundred thirty-four, done.

135.title: Passover: a seat at the seder
135.hook: the seder opens with an invitation: let all who are hungry come and eat
135.howItsDone: Many Jewish families invite friends, partners, neighbors and people who would otherwise be alone to the Passover seder; guests read along from the Haggadah, often in English, and are welcome to ask questions all night.

segments.voice: Yesterday, mishloach manot: food for friends on Purim, and gifts to the poor. Your line was give on the happy day. A month later, the spring festival opens the door.

You met the seder plate on day four. Tonight, imagine you're the one who was invited. A friend's family, a partner's grandparents, a community seder in a rented hall. You sit down, someone hands you a little book, and before anyone has eaten a thing, the leader lifts the flat bread and says, in Aramaic, an old invitation. This is the bread of affliction that our ancestors ate in Egypt. Let all who are hungry come and eat. Before the story, the seder opens the door. Today: what it's like to walk through it.
screen: `YOU'RE INVITED.` → `THE LEADER LIFTS THE MATZAH.` → `ALL WHO ARE HUNGRY, COME.`

segments.voice: Ha lachma anya is said near the start of the seder, in Aramaic, the everyday language of many Jews when it took shape, so that anyone listening would understand the invitation. The whole night is built for people who don't know it yet. The book is the Haggadah, the telling, and many have English beside the Hebrew. People take turns reading, and it's fine to read your part in English. It's long, and dinner comes after a lot of the story, so many guests eat a little something first. There are four cups, and grape juice counts. People lean to the left as they drink, the way free people once reclined at a feast. When the ten plagues are named, people dip a finger or a spoon and take out a drop of wine for each one; many explain that a cup of joy is made less full when others suffer. A piece of matzah, the afikoman, gets hidden, and children hunt for it. Later the door is opened for the prophet Elijah, with a cup poured for him. The songs at the end can get loud. And questions are welcome all night; the Haggadah even makes room for the one who doesn't know how to ask. A practical note: in many homes there's no bread, cake or regular baked goods all week. If you'd like to bring something, ask first. Flowers are always safe.

segments.voice: Picture a long table, set for more people than usual, with a chair for someone who hasn't arrived yet, and the leader lifting the matzah: all who are hungry, come. Think of one person who might not have anywhere to be on a holiday, or a Friday night, or just a Tuesday, and hold them in mind. If you pray, you can pray for them; if not, wish them a full table.
Ha lachma anya. This is the bread of affliction: the Aramaic words over the matzah that open the seder with an invitation to anyone hungry.
Your line: all who are hungry, come. A night about freedom starts by making room at the table. See you tomorrow.

136.title: Counting the Omer (Leviticus 23:15–16)
136.hook: forty-nine days counted from Passover to Shavuot
136.howItsDone: From the second night of Passover, many Jews count the Omer each night after dark: a blessing, then the day and week (today is twelve days, which is one week and five days of the Omer), for forty-nine nights until Shavuot.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ha lachma anya: the seder opens with an invitation to anyone hungry. Your line was all who are hungry, come. The seder is only the first night.

After dark on the second night of Passover, someone stands, says a short blessing, and then says a number. Today is one day of the Omer. The next night, two days. Then three. It goes on every night for seven weeks, out loud, a blessing and a number, until forty-nine. Nothing is crossed off, and nothing is skipped. A sentence that takes ten seconds to say, and a household that has to remember it forty-nine nights in a row. And if someone forgets a night, there's a rule for that too.
screen: `A BLESSING, THEN A NUMBER.` → `EVERY NIGHT FOR SEVEN WEEKS.` → `AND A RULE FOR FORGETTING.`

segments.voice: It comes from the Torah: "And ye shall count unto you" from the day the first sheaf of the harvest was brought to the priest, "seven weeks shall there be complete," and then the fiftieth day is a festival. That first sheaf was the omer, a measure of grain, and it names the whole period: the Omer, and the practice, counting the Omer. Passover falls at the barley harvest; seven weeks later come the wheat harvest and Shavuot. So the count ties two harvests together. Over time, the rabbis also saw it tying two events together: leaving Egypt, and receiving the Torah at Sinai. Leaving slavery, then receiving a way to live. The count is the road between them. The way it's done is precise. Each night after dark, a blessing, then the number: today is twelve days, which is one week and five days of the Omer. You say it, not just think it, and you count up. Forget one night, and you can count the next day, without the blessing. But miss a whole day, and the Shulchan Aruch rules that you keep counting every night, just without the blessing, because the chain was broken. The weeks have a sadder side too. Tradition remembers that many of Rabbi Akiva's students died in this season, so some communities keep signs of mourning, like no weddings, until the thirty-third day, Lag BaOmer, a day of bonfires and joy. In kabbalah, each of the forty-nine days is linked to its own quality to work on, so each day is worth something by itself.

segments.voice: Count your breaths up, slowly, one to seven, and start again; there's no end to rush toward, and each breath is complete in itself. Then think of something you're in the middle of, and say to yourself what day of it this is.
Omer. A sheaf of barley, and the forty-nine days counted aloud, night by night, from Passover to Shavuot.
Your line: count the days up. A habit, a recovery, a new job: every day of it is one more, not one less. That's day one hundred thirty-six.

137.title: Shavuot
137.hook: the day the Torah was given, kept with all-night study and the book of Ruth
137.howItsDone: On Shavuot, many Jews stay up all night studying Torah (Tikkun Leil Shavuot), pray at dawn, read the Ten Commandments and the book of Ruth in synagogue, and eat dairy foods.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Omer: forty-nine nights, counted up out loud. Your line was count the days up. On the fiftieth day, the count arrives.

It's one in the morning, and the synagogue lights are still on. The room is full, and nobody's praying yet. They're studying. Pairs of people bent over books, arguing gently. A teacher at the front with a room of teenagers. Someone's brought a thermos of coffee and a plate of cheesecake. A few people are dozing on the benches. They'll stay until the sky starts to lighten, then pray the morning service at dawn. On this night, staying awake is the whole point.
screen: `ONE IN THE MORNING.` → `A ROOM FULL OF STUDY.` → `AWAKE UNTIL DAWN.`

segments.voice: The holiday is Shavuot, which means weeks: the seven weeks just counted. In the Torah itself, Shavuot is a harvest festival, the day an offering from the new wheat was brought, the day of first fruits. The Torah never says anything else happened on this day. But the rabbis did the math. The Torah says the Israelites reached Mount Sinai in the third month after leaving Egypt, and in the Talmud the sages reckon that the Ten Commandments were given on the sixth of that month, which is Shavuot; one rabbi says the seventh. So in Jewish tradition, Shavuot became the time of the giving of the Torah, the gift at the mountain. One reason given for the all-night study is a midrash: on the morning the Torah was given, the Israelites overslept, and Moses had to wake them. Later, Jewish mystics made a practice of staying up all night on Shavuot, to be awake this time, and the custom spread. It's called a tikkun, a repair. Then there's Ruth. On Shavuot, the book of Ruth is read, a harvest story set during the barley and wheat harvests. Ruth, a woman from Moab, chooses to stay with her mother-in-law Naomi and join her people: "whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge; thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God." One reason given for reading it today: it's the story of someone freely accepting the Torah, as Israel did at Sinai. And Ruth becomes the great-grandmother of King David. There's also a custom of eating dairy foods; the reasons given vary, and no one reason is certain.

segments.voice: Think of the gifts you've been given that you almost slept through: a teacher, a conversation, a book someone pressed into your hands. Pick one, and stay awake with it a little longer, as if this time you won't sleep through it.

Your line: stay up for the gift. Every year, on the fiftieth day, the gift comes round again. Until tomorrow.

138.title: Tisha B'Av
138.hook: a fast of mourning for both Temples and later sorrows, with Lamentations read sitting on the floor
138.howItsDone: On Tisha B'Av, many Jews fast from sunset to nightfall, avoid leather shoes, sit on the floor or low stools, and hear the book of Lamentations and mournful poems (kinot) chanted in dim light.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shavuot: a night awake for the gift of the Torah. Your line was stay up for the gift. Today, the last stop on the walk through the year.

One word, chanted slowly in a dim room: eichah. How. It's the first word of the book of Lamentations, and in Hebrew it's also the book's name. On this summer night the curtain has been taken off the ark. People sit on the floor, or on low stools, some in socks or canvas sneakers. No one greets anyone with a hello. The reader goes on by a small light, verse after verse. The whole room sits low, as if someone has died. In a way, someone has.
screen: `ONE WORD: EICHAH. HOW.` → `THE CURTAIN OFF THE ARK.` → `SITTING ON THE FLOOR.`

segments.voice: Tisha B'Av means the ninth of Av, a day of mourning. On this date, the Mishnah says, both Temples in Jerusalem were destroyed: the first by Babylon, the second by Rome. The Mishnah adds other sorrows to the date, and later tradition remembered more on it, among them the expulsion of the Jews from Spain. So it became the day to mourn many losses at once. It's kept like mourning for a close relative. A fast, from sunset to nightfall, like Yom Kippur, but it gives way to health: anyone ill, pregnant, nursing or at risk asks a doctor and a rabbi. No leather shoes. No washing for pleasure. People sit on the floor or low stools, as mourners do in the week after a funeral. Then comes Lamentations, five short poems of grief over Jerusalem. It opens: "How doth the city sit solitary, that was full of people!" Even Torah study, usually a joy, is limited to sad texts. Still, the day isn't only despair. The rabbis asked why the Second Temple fell, and answered: baseless hatred, people hating each other for nothing. So the day becomes a call to repair. At midday, mourners may rise from the floor. An old tradition says that on Tisha B'Av, of all days, the redeemer is born. And near its end, Lamentations pleads to begin again: "Turn Thou us unto Thee, O LORD, and we shall be turned; renew our days as of old." In the reading, that verse is said again after the last one, so it ends there. That closes the walk through the year, from the calendar and the moon to, today, the floor.
screen: `TISHA B'AV: THE NINTH OF AV.` · `BOTH TEMPLES, AND LATER SORROWS.` · `SITTING LOW, LIKE A MOURNER.` · `BASELESS HATRED, AND A HOPE.` · then, large: `RENEW OUR DAYS AS OF OLD.`

segments.voice: If it's comfortable, lower yourself to the floor; if not, sit low in a chair. Think of one loss you carry, big or small; you don't have to fix it, just let the ground hold you while you hold it. If you pray, you can say Lamentations' old line: renew our days.
Tisha B'Av. The ninth of Av: a fast of mourning for both Temples and later sorrows, with Lamentations read sitting low.
Your line: the floor holds grief. Sitting low lets the ground take some of the weight. Day one hundred thirty-eight.

139.title: What tefillin are (Deuteronomy 6:8)
139.hook: two small leather boxes holding Torah passages, bound on arm and head for weekday morning prayer
139.howItsDone: Many Jews put on tefillin each weekday morning for the morning service, binding one box on the upper arm and one on the head, with blessings. They are not worn on Shabbat or major festivals.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tisha B'Av, the last stop on the walk through the year, sitting low with Lamentations. Your line was the floor holds grief. Now, from the calendar to something worn on the body, every weekday.

Maybe you've seen it in a photo, on a street corner, or at an airport gate early in the morning: someone standing quietly, a prayer shawl over their shoulders, a black leather strap wound around their forearm in neat coils, and a small black box right at the top of their forehead. It can look strange if you've never seen it, even a little severe. But ask the person, and many will tell you it's the most intimate part of their day. For the next five days, i'll open up this one practice, piece by piece.
screen: `A STRAP AROUND THE FOREARM.` → `A BLACK BOX ON THE FOREHEAD.` → `FIVE DAYS, PIECE BY PIECE.`

segments.voice: They're called tefillin, a word usually connected to tefillah, prayer. In English they're sometimes called phylacteries, from a Greek word meaning safeguards, but most Jews just say tefillin. They come from a verse you already know, from the Shema: "And thou shalt bind them for a sign upon thy hand, and they shall be for frontlets between thine eyes." Bind what? The words of God. The rabbis read the verse literally: write the words down and tie them on. So there are two boxes of black leather, perfectly square, each with a leather strap. One is bound on the arm, one on the head. Inside are tiny parchment scrolls, handwritten by a trained scribe with a quill and special ink. They hold four Torah passages: two from Exodus, about remembering the Exodus, and two from Deuteronomy, including the Shema itself. So the verse that says bind these words is itself inside the box. In the head box, the four passages are on four separate scrolls, in four compartments. In the arm box, all four are on one scroll, in one compartment. Tefillin are put on for weekday morning prayer. Not on Shabbat or major festivals, because those days are themselves a sign, the rabbis said, and don't need another. Among the Dead Sea Scrolls, archaeologists found tefillin and their tiny parchments, two thousand years old. And the rabbis taught great care: tefillin are never dropped, they're kept in a bag, and if one falls, many people kiss it when they pick it up.

segments.voice: Choose one thing you want to remember all day, a promise, a person, a value, and put it into a few words. If you have a thread, a hair tie or a rubber band, put it on your hand; if not, press your thumb to one finger. Let the body carry the reminder, so the mind doesn't have to.

140.title: The arm and the heart
140.hook: the arm box sits on the upper arm, facing the heart, so action and feeling join
140.howItsDone: When putting on tefillin, the arm box is placed first on the upper weaker arm, angled toward the heart, with a blessing; its strap is then wound around the forearm, usually seven times.

segments.voice: Yesterday, tefillin: two small boxes holding the words of the Shema, bound as a sign. Your line was bind it as a sign. Today, the first box.

Lift your left arm and bend it, as if to make a muscle. Notice where the top of your arm rests: right up against the side of your chest, close to your heart. If you're left-handed, try it on the right. That spot, the soft part of the upper arm just above the elbow, is exactly where the first box goes. And it isn't placed just anywhere. It's angled, very slightly, so that when the arm is lowered, the box leans in toward the heart.
screen: `BEND YOUR ARM.` → `IT RESTS BY YOUR HEART.` → `THE BOX LEANS INWARD.`

segments.voice: The arm box is called the shel yad, the one of the hand. The Torah says bind them upon thy hand, and the rabbis read hand here as the upper arm, the muscle that moves the hand. They placed it on the weaker arm, the left for a right-handed person, because the verse's wording hinted at it, and so the strong hand could do the binding. The box sits on the bicep, facing the heart. Why the heart? Because another verse, right beside the command about binding, says: "Therefore shall ye lay up these My words in your heart and in your soul; and ye shall bind them for a sign upon your hand." Heart and hand, in one breath. So the rabbis taught that the box on the arm should be across from the heart, and later teachers draw the lesson: the arm is what you do, the heart is what you feel and want, and this practice ties them together. On this reading, a good feeling that never moves the hand falls short, and so does a deed done without the heart. The arm box goes on first, with a blessing. Then the strap is wound around the forearm, usually seven times, down toward the hand. There's also a tradition that the arm box is covered, by a sleeve or the prayer shawl, while the head box is visible: one a private sign, the other a public one. And that's the week: Purim's gifts, the seder's questions, the Omer's count, Shavuot's gift, Tisha B'Av's floor, the boxes, and now the arm against the heart.
screen: `SHEL YAD: THE ONE OF THE HAND.` · `ON THE WEAKER ARM.` · `IN YOUR HEART, UPON YOUR HAND.` · `SEVEN TIMES AROUND THE FOREARM.` · then, large: `HAND AND HEART TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Place one hand flat on your chest and feel your heartbeat, or just the warmth. Think of one thing you have to decide or do today, a message, a conversation, a purchase, and ask two questions: what do I want to do, and what do I actually feel? Wait until they point the same way, or at least until you know where they differ.
Shel yad. The arm box of tefillin, bound on the bicep facing the heart, so what we do and what we feel are tied together.
Your line: hand and heart together. A deed and a feeling, bound in one place. See you tomorrow.
